author: T. S. Eliot
title: Furies in the drawing room
about: Amy, Lady Monchensey, has kept Wishwood, a cold country house in northern England, unchanged for the eight years her eldest son has been away. On her birthday the family gathers and Harry comes home. His wife was lost overboard from a liner a year ago. He says he pushed her, and at the window he sees figures that, he says, the others do not see. Before the night is over he learns what his father once planned, and he leaves the house.

view.says: Following Eliot’s account, Auden wrote that this play went far toward a verse close to speech, though he could not hear the three stresses Eliot counted in each line. The theme, he wrote later, is spiritual election, and Eliot’s comedy convention is bound to make the call seem to come to Harry, and to pass over his brother John for being stupid. He was certain Eliot did not mean it.
view.source: “Eliot on Eliot,” *The Observer*, 28 October 1951, and “T. S. Eliot So Far,” *The Griffin*, March 1953; both in *Prose*, vol. III (2008), pp. 258 and 355

plates.heading: Four views of the play

lenses.label: Line
lenses.what: Two lines of the play with the stresses of speech marked as this page hears them, beside the rule Eliot gave for his line

rule.say: A line of varying length and a varying number of syllables. Three stresses and one pause. Pause and stresses may fall almost anywhere, so long as two of the stresses stand on one side of the pause and one on the other.

aim.say: A rhythm close to the speech of the day, with each stress where a speaker would put it. A verse that needs no prose beside it and can pass without a break from the easiest talk to the most intense speech.

lines.speaker: Amy, heard from offstage
lines.quote: The clock has stopped in the dark!
lines.sides: as marked here, two stresses before the pause and one after it
lines.inThePlay: The last thing Amy says. In the first scene (p. 15) she says that this is what she does not want, and here it has happened.

lines.speaker: Harry
lines.quote: To either of my brothers. Nothing can happen—

mayBeStressed.say: A fifth stress can be heard here. The doctor has just said he hopes the brothers have come to no harm, and Harry’s answer turns on this word.

lines.sides: as marked here, two stresses before the pause and two or three after it
lines.inThePlay: Harry’s answer to the doctor when the police sergeant is announced. It is one of the lines Auden read when he opened the play at random.

auden.say: Auden opened the play at random at this place. He could read none of the lines he found there with fewer than four stresses, and one of them, which appears to be the second line shown, sounded to him like five.

lengths.what: Syllables in each of the twelve lines of the first speech of the play
lengths.speaker: Amy

lenses.caption: Eliot wanted a rhythm close to the speech of his day. By his account the play’s lines vary in length (8 to 16 syllables in the first speech), and each has three stresses, the syllables a speaker leans on, divided two and one by a pause, a caesura. The marks are this page’s hearing, not Eliot’s. By them Amy’s last line keeps the rule. The second line has four stressed words, and can may take a fifth. It stands where Auden opened the play at random: he could read no line there with fewer than four stresses, and heard five in what appears to be this one. On the measuring of verse, he added, each poet thinks only himself right.
lenses.why: Eliot made a line of three stresses and varying length to bring verse close to the speech of his day; Auden could read no line he tried with fewer than four stresses.
lenses.stands: Eliot’s account of the line, in *Poetry and Drama* (1951), p. 27. Syllables counted in the first speech of the play (p. 11) and in the two lines shown (pp. 126 and 78), whose stress marks are this page’s own hearing. Auden’s test of the line, in “Eliot on Eliot” (1951), *Prose*, vol. III, p. 258. Caesura, stress and accent as Baum’s *Principles of English Versification* (1922) defines them.

lenses.what: The six scenes of the play, and the five places in them where two aunts and two uncles speak as a chorus

choruses.together: They ask why they are so uncomfortable, brought together like untrained players whom no one has told what to play, and say that they are here because Amy required it.

apart.name: Gerald

choruses.apartSay: Each names where he or she might have been instead.

choruses.together: They ask why they wait together like plotters who expect to be found out. All they want is to have their fears quieted, and they resolve to keep hold of their settled picture of things.

apart.name: Gerald

choruses.apartSay: Each finds fault with one of the other three, and the four faults make a ring.

choruses.together: Speaking as one, the four say I: afraid of what is past and of what is on its way.

apart.name: Ivy
apart.about: finds such fear beneath her and will not yield to it

apart.name: Charles

choruses.together: A house of long standing takes in and holds whatever has been spoken or endured there. The same unbending rules apply in Argos as at home, and they see no remedy. They end by turning to the evening’s broadcast news.
choruses.apartSay: No one speaks apart. The four go out.

choruses.together: They can manage everyday affairs and hold policies against the common mishaps, though none against what heaven sends. Outside that narrow round they cannot tell what they do or what is done to them, and they say they have missed their way. In a final line all four agree that they must act correctly.

apart.name: Ivy
apart.about: must stay on for the burial, and wonders whether the ticket she holds can still be used

apart.name: Gerald
apart.about: dreads having to face the two younger brothers next day

apart.name: Violet
apart.about: is waiting for the will to be made known

apart.name: Charles
apart.about: feels that some grasp of it all may be within his reach

choruses.apartSay: Three turn to the funeral, the brothers and the will. Charles alone thinks he might come to understand.

lenses.caption: Two aunts and two uncles have parts of their own, and at five places they speak with one voice as a chorus. At all but the fourth, each of them then speaks briefly alone. Together they say they are uneasy, then afraid, then lost. Alone, they speak of a parish tea, of one another’s faults, of an unused ticket. The four are off the stage in the two scenes in which Harry’s pursuers, the Eumenides, are shown. After Murder in the Cathedral Eliot resolved to work the chorus more closely into his next play. He later found the device unsatisfactory, and by Auden’s report more artificial than an outright chorus.
lenses.why: Eliot wanted the chorus to be more a part of the play, so he gave it to four of its persons: together they say they are afraid and lost, and alone each speaks of private concerns or the others’ faults.
lenses.stands: A count of the words spoken under the heading *Chorus* and by the four singly at five places in the 1939 text: pp. 21–22, 42–43, 66–67, 93–94 and 127–29. The stage directions on pp. 60 and 106. Eliot’s aim and later verdict, in *Poetry and Drama* (1951), pp. 25 and 28. Auden’s report of the verdict, in “Eliot on Eliot” (1951), *Prose*, vol. III, p. 258.

lenses.label: Greek
lenses.what: The story of Orestes as Aeschylus tells it, laid beside the play: what Eliot kept and what he changed

facts.under: Aeschylus told the story of Orestes in three plays: the *Agamemnon*, *The Libation-Bearers* and *The Furies*, whose Greek title is the *Eumenides*.

pairs.greek: The house of Atreus, whose people are of Argos. Blow after blow has fallen on it, one generation after another.
pairs.play: Wishwood, a country house in northern England. The chorus names Argos once, beside England (p. 94), Agatha speaks of a curse (pp. 106–07) and tells Harry that the whole family’s burden is now his (p. 102).

pairs.greek: The Furies live in the house. Cassandra, brought to its door, says that they sit within and never leave it.
pairs.play: Harry first sees his pursuers at Wishwood and asks why they waited for him there (p. 24). Later he says they were in the house before he came (p. 106).

pairs.greek: The son, Orestes, comes home from banishment and stands at his father’s grave.
pairs.play: The son, Harry, comes home after eight years and asks the doctor and then his aunt about his dead father (pp. 73–77, 97).

pairs.turn: a killing becomes a plan that was stopped
pairs.greek: A wife kills her husband. Clytemnestra cuts Agamemnon down in his bath.
pairs.play: A husband plans to kill his wife and is stopped. Harry’s father thought of ways to do it three months before Harry was born, and Agatha stopped him (p. 100).

pairs.greek: The son kills his mother, as the god Apollo told him to.
pairs.play: The son says he pushed his wife overboard (p. 29) and later thinks he may have dreamed it (p. 101). His mother dies the same night, after he has gone; her doctor had warned that any great upset might kill her (pp. 76, 126–29).

pairs.greek: The Furies come for him. He sees them and the chorus does not. He tells them so, and runs.
pairs.play: Harry halts in the doorway with his eyes on the window. He asks his family whether they see them, and tells them that they do not and that he does (pp. 23–24).

pairs.greek: A court at Athens tries him. The votes fall equal and he goes free, back to his father’s house. The Furies are given a home under the hill of the court and are called gracious powers.
pairs.play: No court sits. Agatha says the story is one of sin and of atoning for it, and that the sin may not be Harry’s own (p. 101). He stops running and follows his pursuers (pp. 106, 110), in the end gives them a holy name, and leaves the house to his brother (p. 111).

pairs.greek: The chorus is the elders of Argos, then a band of captive women, then the Furies themselves.
pairs.play: The chorus is two aunts and two uncles.

name.means: the gracious goddesses: a euphemism, a kind name used in place of a feared one, for the Erinyes or Furies
name.inThePlay: The name stands in the list of persons and in three stage directions, one on p. 60 and two on p. 106. The Eumenides are shown twice, once on each of those pages. No one in the play speaks the name, and no one says Furies. Harry speaks of them as beings that hunt, pursue and haunt him (pp. 60, 105, 110), and in the end he gives them a holy name (p. 111). His chauffeur takes them for spirits of the dead (p. 125).

eliot.say: Looking back in 1950, Eliot judged that the deepest flaw of the play was a failure to fit the Greek story and the modern situation to each other. He should have kept nearer to Aeschylus, he said, or else taken far more liberty with the myth.

auden.orestes: Auden on the Orestes of Aeschylus, in 1950: his killing of his mother is a duty laid on him and no free choice; he does not repent, and a court acquits him.
auden.harry: Auden on Harry, eighteen years later: he decides on a way of life that may well end in martyrdom.

lenses.caption: Aeschylus’s story of Orestes lies under the play. Eliot keeps its frame: a cursed house, a son come home, pursuers he sees while those around him see no one. In place of its two killings the play has a murder planned and stopped, and a push Harry thinks he may have dreamed. In Aeschylus Orestes does not repent, as Auden noted, and a court tries him and frees him. Here Agatha calls the story one of sin and expiation, of amends for a sin perhaps not Harry’s own, and he turns and follows his pursuers. Eliot later judged that he had not fitted the Greek story to the modern situation.
lenses.why: The play keeps the Greek frame but has no trial: Agatha speaks of sin and of atoning for it, and Harry follows his pursuers. Eliot later judged the Greek story and the modern situation ill adjusted.
lenses.stands: Aeschylus in Morshead’s translation: the [*Agamemnon*](#/read/agamemnon/p5:75), printed here, where Cassandra tells of the Furies of the house; the end of *The Libation-Bearers*; the trial in *The Furies*. The play, pp. 23–24, 29, 100–01, 106 and 110–11. Eliot, *Poetry and Drama*, p. 30. Auden on Orestes, *The Enchafèd Flood*, pp. 109–10. *Expiation* as the Online Etymology Dictionary gives it, and *Eumenides* as Liddell and Scott’s lexicon does.

He saw them before his master did and has grown easy with them. He takes them for spirits of the dead.

He looks and finds nobody there.
He is with the family when Harry tells them that they do not see what he sees. At the end he starts to think there may be something he could grasp, if someone told him.
She is with the family when Harry tells them that they do not see what he sees.
She is with the family when Harry tells them that they do not see what he sees. At the end she says that none of it has made sense to her.

neverArrive.say: On his way to the house he crashes his car in bad weather and is laid up nearby with a head injury.
He telephones from London after an accident. A newspaper reports that a court has fined him and banned him from driving for a year.

election.means: In its religious sense the word is God’s choice of a person for eternal life.
election.say: Harry’s own word for what has come to him. He says he cannot tell why it is his. Agatha has told him that he is chosen (p. 102).

john.heading: What is said of John, who is to have the house

said.say: the least quick of the three brothers
so little awake at the best of times that a knock on the head changes little
likely to settle in the family house and marry someone duller than he is
to take Harry’s place as head of the house, with everything that was his

audience.in1939: In the 1939 text the audience sees them twice, when the stage directions show them at the window.
audience.later: Eliot said in 1950 that in future they should be left out of the cast and taken to be seen by some of the characters and not by the audience.

auden.say: Auden: the theme is spiritual election. The play takes over the convention of English high comedy, whose chief persons are aristocrats, and that convention is bound to make it seem that Harry is the one called, and that his brother John is passed over for being stupid. He was certain Eliot did not mean it.

lenses.caption: Harry sees his pursuers, the Eumenides, at the window. His aunt Agatha, his cousin Mary and his chauffeur see them too. His mother and the chorus do not, and his brothers never arrive. Harry speaks of his election, his being chosen, and cannot say why it is his. John, who gets the house, is called dependable, dull and barely aware. Auden wrote that the play takes over the convention of English high comedy, where wealth and breeding can stand for gifts and virtues. When the theme is spiritual election, it is bound to seem that Harry, not John, is called because John is stupid. Auden was certain Eliot did not mean it.
lenses.why: Only some of the house see the Eumenides, and Harry speaks of his election; Auden wrote that the comedy convention is bound to make the call seem to go by brains, against Eliot’s meaning.
lenses.stands: The play: pp. 23–24, 60–61, 106, 110, 117 and 125 for who sees them; pp. 81 and 89–92 for the brothers’ accidents; pp. 102 and 111 for Harry’s being chosen; pp. 77, 84, 87, 95 and 111 for what is said of John. The religious sense of *election* as the Online Etymology Dictionary gives it. Auden, “T. S. Eliot So Far” (1953), *Prose*, vol. III, p. 355.

plates.noTextWhy: The play is in copyright in the United States through 2034, so its text cannot be printed here. Two of its lines are quoted for study. Everything else is counted or described from the New York edition of 1939.

auden.says: Reviewing Eliot’s lecture in 1951, Auden follows his account of the play. Eliot had decided to take a subject from his own time, to find a verse rhythm near its speech, and to let the characters do the commenting. In this play, he writes, Eliot went far toward solving the problem of the verse. Then Auden tries the rule of three stresses on lines found by opening the play at random, and can read none with fewer than four. On prosody, the measuring of verse, he adds, each poet thinks only himself right. He reports Eliot’s verdict: letting the characters comment had proved more artificial than an outright chorus.
auden.source: “Eliot on Eliot,” a review of Eliot’s *Poetry and Drama*, *The Observer*, 28 October 1951; in *Prose*, vol. III (2008), pp. 257–59

auden.says: Reviewing Eliot’s collected poems and plays in 1953, Auden says that in the plays the chosen persons, Becket, Harry and Celia, take their suffering as a way to grace and a sign of special vocation. If this play and *The Cocktail Party* sound a snobbish note at times, he puts it down to technique. Intent on a stage verse that would not be arty, Eliot put off the question of convention and took over that of English high comedy, whose chief persons are aristocrats. That serves while the subject is worldly, since wealth and breeding can stand for gifts and virtues. For a theme of spiritual election it breaks down.
auden.source: “T. S. Eliot So Far,” a review of Eliot’s *Complete Poems and Plays*, *The Griffin*, March 1953; in *Prose*, vol. III (2008), pp. 352–55

auden.says: In the foreword to his T. S. Eliot Memorial Lectures of 1967, Auden sets Harry beside two other persons of Eliot’s plays. Becket, in the first long play, was a martyr known to history. What becomes of Harry is not told, Auden says, but he decides on a way of life that may well end in martyrdom, as Celia’s decision does in *The Cocktail Party*.
auden.source: *Secondary Worlds* (New York: Random House, 1968), Foreword, p. 11

auden.says: In a book of 1950, writing about heroes of revenge, Auden describes the Orestes of Aeschylus, whose story lies under the play. His killing of his mother is no free choice: it is a duty that comes to him from what he owes his father. What the Furies make him suffer is unexpected and comes from nothing in himself. He does not repent, and a divine court acquits him. Auden is not writing about Eliot’s play here.
auden.source: *The Enchafèd Flood* (1950; Vintage Books edition, 1967), pp. 109–10

caveats: What Auden says here was written between 1950 and 1968, nine to twenty-seven years after his course of 1941, and his remark on Orestes is not about this play. No record was found of anything he said about the play in class.
Auden’s two reviews and his foreword were read for this page in short passages of scanned copies, not in full.

The stress marks on the two lines are this page’s own, and each line can be heard another way. Eliot marked the stresses of no line of the play in his lecture, and Auden gave only counts. Which line he heard with five stresses is inferred from his count.
The play was read in a later printing of the New York edition of 1939. Page numbers are that printing’s, and other printings and editions may differ.

The counts were made on that copy: for the chorus, words, with lines that turn over on the page joined and a hyphenated name counted as one; for the first speech, syllables, where a word that can be said in one syllable or two was counted as one.
